title: First Date Tips: Planning, What to Talk About and Staying Safe — cv.cm
description: Practical first date tips: where to go and for how long, who pays, a list of questions to ask, what not to do, safety steps, consent and how to end the date.
h1: What are the best first date tips?
answer: Pick a public place where you can talk, and plan about one to two hours. Ask open questions and follow up on the answers, share about yourself too, and put your phone away. Keep alcohol low, tell a friend where you are, and get there on your own. End clearly and kindly, and say if you would like to meet again.

sections.h: What a first date is for
body: A first date is not a test you pass or fail. It is a short meeting to answer two questions: do I enjoy this person, and do they seem to enjoy me? Keeping that in mind takes away a lot of pressure. You do not need to be perfect, funny all the time, or say the right things. You need to be present and honest.

It also helps to know that people usually think a first meeting went worse than it did. Research by Erica Boothby and colleagues found that after talking with someone new, people tend to underestimate how much the other person liked them. If you leave thinking "I talked too much" or "that was awkward", the other person may remember it much more warmly.

body: Who pays depends on the country, the couple and the situation. In some places the person who invited usually pays; in others splitting the bill is normal; some couples take turns. A simple, respectful approach: the person who asked offers to pay, and if the other person wants to split, accept that. Do not make paying feel like the other person now owes you anything.
Confirm the day before with a short message: "Looking forward to tomorrow. Still good for 3 pm at the cafe?" It is polite and lets either of you change plans early.

The best conversations go back and forth. A study by Karen Huang and colleagues found that people who asked more follow-up questions, questions about what the other person had just said, were liked more, and in speed dating they got more second dates. So ask, listen, then ask about the answer.

Arthur Aron's well-known "36 questions" study showed that strangers who took turns sharing slowly more personal things felt much closer afterward. You do not need to use a list on a date, but the idea helps: start light, share something of your own, and go a little deeper as it feels comfortable.

ul: Light: "How do you usually spend your weekends?" "What's the best thing you ate recently?"
Interests: "How did you get into climbing?" "What do you like about that show?"
Stories: "What's a trip you still think about?" "What were you like as a kid?"
Plans and dreams: "Is there something you've wanted to learn for a long time?"
Follow-ups: "Wait, how did that happen?" "What did you do next?" "Why that city?"

body: Topics to keep for later dates: past relationships in detail, money problems, health details, and heavy political or religious debates. You can mention them briefly if they come up, but a first date is not the place to go deep.

ul: Look at your phone often. Put it away and check only if you need to.
Talk only about yourself, or only ask questions and never share.
Talk a lot about your ex.
Drink a lot to calm your nerves.
Comment on their body or try to touch them without a clear signal that it is welcome.
Treat staff badly. How you treat a waiter says a lot about you.
Push for a second date, a kiss or going somewhere else when they seem unsure.
Pretend to be someone else. It only delays the moment you find out if you fit.

body: Safety matters most when you met online and have not met before, but it is a good habit for any first date. love is respect recommends choosing a public place, telling a friend or family member your plans, and arranging your own transport so you decide when your home address is shared.

ol: Meet in a busy public place, and stay in public for the first date.
Tell a friend where you are going, who you are meeting, and when you expect to be home. Message them when you leave.
Get there and back on your own: your own car, a taxi you booked, or public transport.
Keep alcohol low and do not leave your drink alone.
Trust your feelings. If something feels wrong, you can leave. Say "I need to go now" and go. You do not owe anyone an explanation.
Never send money to someone you have just met or only know online.

body: Consent means both people agree, freely and clearly, to what happens, and either person can change their mind at any time. love is respect describes it as an ongoing, mutual agreement about what you both want, not just waiting for someone to say no.

On a first date, that can be very simple. Before a hug or a kiss, you can ask: "Can I give you a hug?" or "Can I kiss you?" A clear yes, said or shown, is a yes. Silence, pulling back, looking away or a hesitant "um" is not. If they say no or not yet, say "Of course" and carry on warmly. Respecting that makes people feel safe with you, which is attractive in itself.

body.note: Alcohol does not change the rules. A person who is very drunk cannot give real consent.

body: Plan an end so neither person has to guess. When the time feels right, say something clear.

faq.q: How long should a first date last?
faq.a: About one to two hours is common. It is long enough to talk and short enough that neither of you feels stuck.

faq.q: Is it okay to kiss on the first date?
faq.a: Yes, if you both want to. Look for clear signs and ask if you are unsure. Not kissing is also completely normal.

faq.q: What should I wear on a first date?
faq.a: Something clean that fits the place and that you feel comfortable in. You will talk better if you are not thinking about your clothes.

faq.q: What if there is an awkward silence?
faq.a: Short silences are normal. Ask a follow-up about something they said earlier, or comment on something around you.

faq.q: Should I tell my date I am nervous?
faq.a: Yes, if you want to. "I'm a bit nervous, I don't do this often" is honest and often makes both people relax.
